lessons.title: Hands-on Substrate Preparation
lessons.body:
Start by gathering materials for 50 kg of substrate. You need 40 kg of dry chopped cereal straw (wheat, rice, or barley), 5 kg of cotton seed hulls if available, 2 kg of gypsum, and 1 kg of lime. Also prepare a clean 200-litre drum for pasteurisation, a large tarpaulin, and a water source. Chop straw to 3â5 cm pieces. In a wheelbarrow, mix dry straw, gypsum, and lime thoroughly. Add water gradually while turning until the mixture holds together when squeezed but no water drips outâabout 65â70% moisture. This takes roughly 60 litres of water. Heap the wet mixture under a tarpaulin for 24 hours to absorb moisture evenly.

Next, pasteurise the substrate to kill competitors. Fill the drum halfway with water and heat to 80Â°C. Place the soaked substrate into a porous sack or wire basket and submerge it in the hot water. Maintain 70â80Â°C for 60 minutes. Do not boil, as this can break down nutrients. Alternatively, use a simple steam pasteurisation: place substrate on a raised platform inside a sealed drum with a small water layer at the bottom, heat until steam escapes for 30 minutes. After pasteurisation, drain the substrate on a clean, disinfected surface (e.g., plastic sheet wiped with 70% alcohol). Let it cool to below 30Â°C (test with a clean handâshould feel barely warm).

Now check moisture again. If too dry, add a little clean water; if too wet, spread and air-dry for 30 minutes. The final substrate should be dark, earthy-smelling, and not slimy. Pack it into clean plastic bags or trays. For a small grow room, fill 10 bags of 5 kg each. Work in a shaded, dust-free area. Avoid touching the substrate with bare hands after pasteurisationâuse clean gloves. This process takes about 4 hours from start to finish. With practice, you can prepare 50 kg in one morning. Remember: contamination comes from dirty tools, hands, or water. Always sanitise everything.

lessons.title: Inoculation Practice
lessons.body:
Inoculation is mixing mushroom spawn into cooled substrate. Work in a clean, still-air room. Wear clean clothes, wash hands with soap, and put on disposable gloves. Wipe all surfaces with 70% alcohol. You need mushroom spawn (e.g., oyster or button) at 5â10% of substrate weight. For 5 kg of substrate, use 250â500 g of spawn. Break spawn into small piecesâabout the size of a thumbâusing clean hands or a sterile spoon. Do not crush it.

Open your substrate bag or tray. Sprinkle spawn evenly over the surface, then mix gently but thoroughly so spawn is distributed throughout the substrate. Do not overmixâjust 3â4 turns. For bag culture, you can layer: one-third substrate, one-third spawn, repeat, ending with substrate. Close the bag with a clean rubber band or tie, leaving a small filter for air (e.g., a cotton plug). For trays, cover with a clean plastic sheet with small holes. Label each bag with date and spawn type.

After inoculation, place bags in a dark, warm room at 25â28Â°C and 80â85% humidity. Do not open bags for 10â14 days. You will see white mycelium spreading. If you see green, black, or pink patches, remove that bag immediatelyâit is contaminated. For the first 3 days, check temperature daily; if too hot, open a window or use a fan indirectly. After 10 days, the substrate should be fully white. This is called 'spawn run'. Now move bags to the fruiting room with light and lower temperature (18â24Â°C). Cut small slits in bags for mushrooms to emerge. Mist twice daily. In 5â7 days, pins (tiny mushrooms) appear. Harvest when caps are fully open but before spores drop. This hands-on practice is the heart of mushroom farmingâdo it carefully, and you will succeed.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Small Grow Room
lessons.body:
Choose a room that is easy to clean, has no direct sunlight, and can be closed off. A spare bedroom, shed, or corner of a garage works. Size: for 20 bags (5 kg each), you need about 2 m x 2 m floor space with shelves. You will need: plastic sheeting to cover walls and floor, wooden or metal shelves (3â4 tiers), a humidifier or hand sprayer, a thermometer, a hygrometer (measures humidity), a small fan, and a light source (fluorescent tube or LED). Also a cleanable table for inoculation.

First, clean the room thoroughly. Remove all dust and debris. Wipe walls and floor with a disinfectant (1 part bleach to 10 parts water). Cover walls and floor with plastic sheeting for easy cleaning. Install shelves leaving 40 cm between tiers. Place a thermometer and hygrometer at mid-height. For humidity, you can use a simple humidifier (ultrasonic) or manually mist 2â3 times daily. Aim for 80â85% during spawn run and 85â90% during fruiting. For temperature, oyster mushrooms prefer 18â24Â°C; button mushrooms 16â20Â°C. In hot African climates, you may need a small air conditioner or evaporative cooler. In cooler areas, a heater may be needed. Use a fan on low speed to circulate air, but avoid direct wind on bags.

Light: mushrooms need indirect light for fruiting. A 20-watt fluorescent tube 1.5 m above shelves for 12 hours daily is enough. Do not use direct sunlight. Keep the room dark during spawn run (first 10â14 days). After opening bags, provide light. Also maintain hygiene: no shoes inside, wear clean lab coat or apron, wash hands before entering. Keep a spray bottle of 70% alcohol to sanitise tools. Monitor daily: check temperature, humidity, and any signs of contamination. A small notebook to record data helps. Total setup cost in many African cities: plastic sheeting $10, shelves $30, humidifier $25, thermometer/hygrometer $10, light $15, fan $15âabout $105. You can start with 10 bags and expand. This room can produce 3â5 kg of mushrooms per week within a month.

lessons.title: Harvesting and Packaging Simulation
lessons.body:
Harvest mushrooms when they are fully grown but before spores release. For oyster mushrooms, the caps should be flat or slightly upturned, edges smooth. For button mushrooms, harvest when caps are closed but gills not visible. Do not wait until they turn brown or slimy. Harvest in the morning when cool. Wash hands and use a clean, sharp knife or scissors. Twist the mushroom gently at the base and cut, leaving a small stub. Do not pull, as this damages the substrate. Place mushrooms in a clean basket or trayânot plastic bags, which cause sweating. Harvest all mature mushrooms at once. For a 5 kg bag, you might get 1â1.5 kg in the first flush. After harvest, mist the substrate and wait for a second flush in 7â10 days. You can get 3â4 flushes.

After harvesting, clean mushrooms. Remove any substrate bits with a soft brush or damp cloth. Do not wash with waterâmushrooms absorb water and spoil faster. Sort by size and quality: Grade A (uniform, unblemished), Grade B (slightly uneven), Grade C (for processing). For packaging, use food-grade plastic containers, paper bags, or cling film. In many African markets, 250 g or 500 g punnets are popular. Weigh accurately. For 250 g, use a small scale. Pack mushrooms stem down, caps up, in a single layer. For oyster mushrooms, you can bundle 3â4 together. Label with harvest date and weight. Store at 4Â°C (refrigerator) for up to 7 days. Without refrigeration, sell within 24 hours. For transport, use a cool box with ice packs. Simulate a market sale: set a price. In Kenya, oyster mushrooms retail at KES 400â600 per kg; in Nigeria, NGN 2,000â3,000 per kg. Practice packaging 10 punnets of 250 g each. This simulation teaches you speed and hygiene. Remember: bruised mushrooms lose value. Handle gently.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Real Cases
lessons.body: Case 1: Green mould on substrate. This is Trichoderma, a common competitor. Cause: insufficient pasteurisation, dirty tools, or too high humidity. Solution: remove and bury contaminated bags far from grow room. Increase pasteurisation time to 90 minutes. Clean room with bleach solution. In future, add 1% lime to substrate. Case 2: Mushrooms are long and thin with small caps. Cause: too much carbon dioxide, not enough fresh air. Solution: increase ventilationâopen door for 10 minutes twice daily or use fan on low. Also reduce humidity to 85%. Case 3: No mushrooms after 3 weeks. Cause: spawn run not complete, temperature too low, or spawn too old. Solution: check for white mycelium; if present, wait another week. If not, re-inoculate with fresh spawn. Ensure temperature is 18â24Â°C. Case 4: Mushrooms have brown spots. Cause: bacterial blotch from too much water on caps. Solution: water only the substrate, not mushrooms. Improve air circulation. Case 5: Substrate smells sour. Cause: anaerobic bacteria from over-wet substrate. Solution: discard; next time, drain substrate well after pasteurisation. Case 6: Mushrooms are small and dry. Cause: low humidity or insufficient water. Solution: mist more often, aim for 85â90% humidity. Case 7: Insects (flies, mites). Cause: open doors, dirty environment. Solution: use fine mesh on windows, keep room clean, use sticky traps. Case 8: Mushrooms taste bitter. Cause: harvesting too late or substrate with too much gypsum. Solution: harvest earlier, reduce gypsum to 1 kg per 50 kg. For each case, record what you did. Share with other farmers. In Africa, common problems are heat and contamination. Simple fixes often work: shade, ventilation, and hygiene. Practice diagnosing by looking at symptoms. If unsure, ask an experienced grower or extension officer.

lessons.title: Field Trip to a Commercial Farm
lessons.body:
Arrange a visit to a commercial mushroom farm near you. Look for farms that grow oyster, button, or shiitake mushrooms. Call ahead and ask for a tour. Bring a notebook, pen, and camera (if allowed). Wear clean clothes and shoes that can be disinfected. On arrival, observe the layout: where is the substrate preparation area? How do they pasteurise? What materials do they use? Ask about their production scale: how many bags per week? What is their yield per bag? For example, a commercial farm might produce 100 kg per week from 500 bags. Note their spawn sourceâdo they make their own or buy? Ask about costs: substrate materials, labour, electricity, water. In Kenya, a 5 kg bag might cost KES 150 to produce and sell for KES 400. In Nigeria, similar ratios.

Observe hygiene practices: do workers wear gloves, masks, and clean coats? How do they enter the grow room? Is there a footbath? How do they control temperature and humidity? Look for equipment: autoclave, humidifiers, air conditioners, shelving. Ask about problems: what are their biggest challenges? Common answers: contamination, heat, market access, and transport. Ask how they solve them. For example, they might use solar-powered fans or evaporative cooling. Ask about harvesting and packaging: how do they grade? What packaging do they use? Where do they sellâsupermarkets, restaurants, hotels, direct? What price do they get? Note their record-keeping: do they track daily temperature, humidity, yields? Ask if they keep a logbook.

After the tour, sit down and write your observations. Compare with your own small grow room. What can you improve? Maybe better ventilation, a cleaner inoculation area, or a simple record system. Ask if you can volunteer for a day to learn hands-on. Many farmers are willing to share if you show respect. Also ask about their market linkagesâwho buys their mushrooms? Can they connect you? Finally, calculate the economics: if you produce 5 kg per week and sell at KES 500 per kg, that is KES 2,500 per week. After costs, profit might be KES 1,500. This field trip is your best teacher. Take photos, ask questions, and network. When you return, implement at least three new ideas in your own farm.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for mushroom substrate before pasteurisation?
quiz.explanation: Substrate should hold together when squeezed but not drip water, which is about 65â70% moisture.

quiz.q: How long should substrate be pasteurised in hot water at 70â80Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Pasteurisation at 70â80Â°C for 60 minutes kills competitors without destroying nutrients.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spawn rate for mushroom cultivation?
quiz.explanation: Using 5â10% spawn ensures rapid colonisation and reduces contamination risk.

quiz.q: During spawn run, what temperature range is ideal for most mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Most mushroom mycelium grows best at 25â28Â°C during the spawn run phase.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see green mould on a substrate bag?
options: C) Remove and bury the bag far away
quiz.explanation: Green mould is Trichoderma; remove contaminated bags immediately to prevent spread.

quiz.q: How often should you mist mushrooms during fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Misting twice daily maintains high humidity needed for fruiting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of covering grow room walls with plastic sheeting?
quiz.explanation: Plastic sheeting makes surfaces smooth and easy to disinfect, reducing contamination.

quiz.q: Which light source is suitable for a small mushroom grow room?
quiz.explanation: Indirect, low-intensity light from a fluorescent tube promotes fruiting without overheating.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity range during fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Fruiting mushrooms need high humidity, around 85â90%, to develop properly.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid washing mushrooms with water after harvest?
options: B) They absorb water and spoil faster
D) It makes them taste bitter
quiz.explanation: Mushrooms are like sponges; washing with water shortens shelf life.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to harvest oyster mushrooms?
options: B) Cut with clean knife leaving small stub
quiz.explanation: Cutting with a clean knife avoids damaging the substrate and allows further flushes.

quiz.q: How many flushes can you typically get from one substrate bag?
quiz.explanation: With proper care, a substrate bag can produce 3â4 flushes over several weeks.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of long, thin mushrooms with small caps?
quiz.explanation: High CO2 from poor ventilation causes mushrooms to stretch seeking oxygen.

quiz.q: What should you do if substrate smells sour?
quiz.explanation: Sour smell indicates anaerobic bacteria; the substrate is spoiled and should be discarded.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of bacterial blotch on mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Brown spots on caps are typical of bacterial blotch, often from water on caps.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to prevent insects in the grow room?
options: C) Install fine mesh on windows
quiz.explanation: Fine mesh blocks flies and mites while allowing air circulation.

quiz.q: Why might mushrooms taste bitter?
options: B) Too much gypsum in substrate
quiz.explanation: Excess gypsum can cause bitterness; reduce to 1 kg per 50 kg substrate.

quiz.q: What is the first step when visiting a commercial mushroom farm?
options: B) Call ahead and ask for a tour
quiz.explanation: Calling ahead ensures someone is available and respects biosecurity.

quiz.q: What should you observe about a commercial farm's substrate preparation?
quiz.explanation: Learning their pasteurisation and materials helps you improve your own process.

quiz.q: What is a common challenge for commercial mushroom farms in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Heat and contamination are frequently cited as major challenges.

quiz.q: What should you do after a field trip?
options: B) Write observations and implement three ideas
quiz.explanation: Reflecting and applying at least three new ideas maximises learning.

quiz.q: How can a small grow room maintain high humidity without a humidifier?
options: B) Mist walls and floor twice daily
quiz.explanation: Misting walls and floor increases humidity through evaporation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shelf spacing in a grow room?
quiz.explanation: 40 cm between tiers allows air circulation and easy access.

quiz.q: Which mushroom species prefers 16â20Â°C for fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Button mushrooms fruit best at slightly cooler temperatures than oyster.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding gypsum to substrate?
options: B) To provide calcium and improve structure
quiz.explanation: Gypsum provides calcium and helps keep substrate particles separate.

quiz.q: How should you label inoculated bags?
options: A) With date and spawn type
quiz.explanation: Date and spawn type help track spawn run and identify problems.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of successful spawn run?
quiz.explanation: White mycelium growing through substrate indicates healthy colonisation.

quiz.q: When should you cut slits in bags for fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Wait until substrate is fully white (10â14 days) before introducing fruiting conditions.

quiz.q: What is a good packaging size for retail mushrooms in Africa?
quiz.explanation: 250 g punnets are popular for household purchase.

quiz.q: How long can fresh mushrooms be stored at 4Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Refrigeration at 4Â°C extends shelf life to about one week.
